body_markdown:
A young engineer from Uruguay is rewriting the hypercar rulebook. Santiago Sánchez Rivero’s Sanrivatti One features a novel driving position that takes inspiration from the world of motorcycling.


It’s called the Apex Position, and it puts the pilot in a head-forward pose, with arms ahead and legs behind, and promises a new level of connection between car and driver—or maybe that should be rider?


Rivero grew up with motorcycles, but from the age of just 14, his heart was set on building his own hypercar. He moved to the Netherlands to study motorsport and automotive engineering and, along the way, came up with the idea to combine his two passions.


Sanrivatti


“I didn’t agree or like the way that the industry was going in the hypercar sector. It was going more towards spec sheets and numbers, and I feel that we forgot the essence of why do people drive?” says Rivero. “I want to bring something new to this industry, and I started going back to my childhood, and that’s when I started thinking about motocross and motorcycles. Why are bikes so immediate? Why do you feel that connection? You don’t have that on a car, and that’s what I started questioning. Of course, a bike is lower weight, and you have the engine between your legs, but there has to be something more to it, not just weight and power. That’s when the Apex Position came up: What if we adopt a head-forward driver position, but inside a car?”


Sanrivatti


According to Rivero’s simulations, one major advantage compared to a conventional driving position is the visibility that Apex provides. In experiments, the Apex Position delivered a 28-degree vertical field of view, compared to just 15.5 degrees for a benchmark hypercar.


That sounds encouraging, but how, exactly, would someone drive (or ride) in this position? The answer is what Sanrivatti calls its G-Force Neutralizing System.


“In most cars—well, every car—your weight is dead weight; what we’re doing is making that weight active weight. So now you’re countering the G-Forces that you experience in the car and going with it. So you feel way more connected than ever before,” adds Rivero.


In practical terms, this means that the driver leans into corners, like on a motorcycle, although this weight transfer isn’t used to actually steer the car as it would be on two wheels. Instead, there’s a conventional steering wheel, while braking and acceleration are controlled by the pedals behind the driver.


Rivero admits there’ll be quite a steep learning curve. “We’re doing something that no one has done before, so no one has experience in driving this type of vehicle. What we’re doing is we’re also giving our clients a driver program—a club—where we teach you how to drive this car. It’s not a motorcycle, it’s not a car, it’s something completely new. So you have to learn how this car behaves, not only the controls, but also how to feel the car through this new position.”


The Sanrivatti One will be track-only, and Rivero is also planning exclusive circuit experiences for customers to experience the full performance of the car. It certainly won’t be slow, with power coming from a 5.5-liter, 800-hp Judd V-10 engine, driving the rear wheels through a six-speed sequential Hewland transmission. It’s set to top 200 mph and weigh just 2425 lbs.


Sanrivatti


Suspension is by double wishbones with pushrods, while AP Racing brakes, Braid forged magnesium wheels, and Michelin racing tires make for an impressive list of suppliers,


The One will be built around a carbon fiber tub, with its bodywork said to be inspired by fighter aircraft and the dive of a peregrine falcon.


It may all sound fanciful, but Rivero has built a credible team to drive the project, including former Singer Vehicle Design and McLaren executive Paul Arkesden as Executive Director of Technology Partnerships, and former Lotus, Bentley and Harley-Davidson executive Geoff Dowding as Commercial Strategic Advisor.


With the first prototype and design model (below) just revealed, Rivero says the company will work through an extensive testing and development program before it delivers its first customer car in 2030.
